You don’t just place any fence that separates them—you slide it so that the empty buffer (a corridor) between the fence and the closest points on either side is as wide as possible. That corridor’s width is the “margin.”

- Key idea: The classifier must separate all training points with zero mistakes, and among all such separators it chooses the one with the largest margin. Only a few boundary points (the closest ones on each side) actually “pin” the fence in place; these are the support vectors.

- When it works well: Data are clean and linearly separable (no overlap). It tends to generalize better than a just‑barely separating line because a wider margin usually means more robustness to small perturbations.

- Limitations: It’s brittle to outliers—one mislabeled or extreme point can force a bad fence or make perfect separation impossible. When data aren’t perfectly separable, you switch to the “soft‑margin” version, which allows small violations.

- Extensions: If a straight fence isn’t enough, you can map data to a higher‑dimensional space (via kernels) and still apply the same “max‑gap” idea there.
